## The Problem

NBA news apps give you headlines, but not a sense of how fans are actually reacting to a story. I wanted to build an aggregator that paired each headline with real fan sentiment, not just the article itself.

## What I Built and Why

A Next.js news aggregator that pulls headlines from ESPN and CBS Sports, scores sentiment, and was meant to back that sentiment with real comments matched to each specific story. I built the comment pipeline against YouTube first (Reddit and Twitter/X both locked down free real-time API access years ago, so YouTube was the only realistic free option), including a relevance-scoring system meant to confirm a video was actually about the same story before pulling its comments. I also put real engineering work into making it production-ready: parallelized the sentiment pipeline to cut cold-load time from 15 seconds to 4, fixed real bugs, cleaned up dead code, and added PWA support.

## How It Went

Even with the relevance scoring, the YouTube comments often came from videos that weren't actually about the linked article, since there's no reliable way to programmatically tie a YouTube video to a specific, recent news story. That's a structural data problem, not a bug I could patch. Combined with Reddit and Twitter being closed off, the core idea (sentiment tied accurately to a specific story) wasn't achievable without a paid data source. I stopped active development at that point. The core news aggregator still works and is still live.

## What I'd Do Differently

I'd validate the comment-to-article matching as a tiny proof of concept before building the rest of the pipeline around it. I spent real time on performance and polish for a feature whose core data problem I hadn't actually confirmed was solvable yet.

## Tech Stack

Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Supabase, YouTube Data API, OpenAI (optional sentiment), Sentry
